title: The Hallucination Tracker
creator: Hallucination-Free
scope: 51 selected records spanning documented milestones in 2022–2026, including four controlled studies, one labelled lawsuit allegation and one labelled first-person forum report. Verifying a reported claim does not establish its truth or causation. Partial source access and attribution are noted per record. Not exhaustive, representative, a prevalence estimate or a trend measure. Prevention fields are editorial analysis. CC BY covers original summaries and compilation, not linked sources.

records.title: Air Canada: chatbot advice contradicted the fare policy
records.date_basis: Month of chatbot interaction; tribunal decision dated 2024-02-14.
records.organization: Air Canada
records.system: Website chatbot; model and architecture not established by the passages reviewed
records.what_happened: The tribunal describes a chatbot advising that bereavement fares could be requested retroactively, followed by employees saying they could not. The passenger sought the fare difference.
records.impact: The tribunal found negligent misrepresentation and mostly allowed the claim. Dentons’ February 15, 2024 summary reports an award of $650.88, essentially the fare difference; this amount is attributed to that secondary account because the complete primary disposition was not recovered.
records.response: The decision records Air Canada denying liability, disputing retroactive eligibility and seeking dismissal (paragraph 4). Paragraph 22 records a company response acknowledging misleading chatbot wording. Dentons reports a February 2023 email saying the issue was noted for a chatbot update; that establishes an intention, not a verified completed fix.
records.response_status: Company position and acknowledgement recorded in tribunal decision
records.prevention_analysis: Generate fare eligibility from a versioned approved policy decision, and prevent unsupported prose from promising an exception. Conflicting advice should route to review before the traveler relies on it. This is a proposed control, not a finding about the unknown chatbot implementation.
records.source_scope: Tribunal decision on third-party host. Indexed heading and paragraphs 1–11 plus recovered same-document passages 22 and 28; complete order unavailable. Supplementary indexed Dentons passages on the award and airline email: https://www.dentonsdata.com/airline-ordered-to-compensate-a-b-c-man-because-its-chatbot-provided-inaccurate-information/.

records.title: Bard: a launch advertisement misidentified the first exoplanet image
records.date_basis: Advertisement episode reported February 8, 2023; exact GIF publication day not recovered.
records.organization: Google / Alphabet
records.system: Google Bard; exact demonstration configuration not verified
records.what_happened: Reuters reported that a Google promotional GIF showed Bard incorrectly crediting the James Webb Space Telescope with the first pictures of an exoplanet. NASA identifies 2M1207 b as first imaged with the Very Large Telescope in 2004 and confirmed in 2005.
records.impact: Reuters reported roughly $100 billion in lost Alphabet market value on February 8 amid both the inaccurate advertisement and an underwhelming presentation. This does not isolate the answer’s causal contribution to the share movement.
records.response: A Google spokesperson said the error showed the need for rigorous testing and described a Trusted Tester program combining external feedback with internal testing for quality, safety and factual grounding.
records.response_status: Response reported in the linked source
records.prevention_analysis: Before publishing a generated demonstration, verify each scientific milestone against the original agency record. Block publication when the telescope, date or claimed first cannot be supported. This is an editorial control proposal, not proven prevention.
records.source_scope: Partial indexed Reuters account on Yahoo; NASA correction at https://science.nasa.gov/resource/2m1207-b-first-image-of-an-exoplanet/; indexed company response reported by Business Today. Original Reuters and Space.com URLs were unreadable.

records.title: Mata v. Avianca: fabricated authorities in a court filing
records.date_basis: Filing date identified in the court order; not the date of model generation.
records.organization: Levidow, Levidow & Oberman P.C.
records.system: ChatGPT, as identified by the court; version not verified
records.what_happened: The court describes nonexistent opinions, with fabricated quotations and citations generated by ChatGPT, being submitted and then defended after their existence was questioned.
records.impact: The court required production of the cited opinions and issued a show-cause order. This record does not quantify sanctions because the disposition was not accessible in this review.
records.response: The court records that respondents stood by the opinions after judicial orders questioned them. A separate case-specific firm or developer statement was not verified; the court account is not a direct statement from them. Recovered court passages date the defendant’s challenge to March 15, production orders to April 11–12 and the start of disclosure to May 25, 2023.
records.response_status: Court account only; separate statement unverified
records.prevention_analysis: A filing gate requiring a reviewer to retrieve each original authority and verify its quotation and proposition would reject citations that cannot be substantiated. An unresolved authority must block filing; a generated assurance is not evidence.
records.source_scope: Substantive indexed opening only; complete opinion and disposition not retrieved. Batch 1 re-read recovered procedural chronology, but not the final penalty.

records.title: ChatGPT: a false account of Brian Hood’s role in a bribery scandal
records.date_basis: Public-report month; ABC’s URL is April 6, with recovered metadata showing April 5 without timezone. Exact interaction date unknown.
records.organization: OpenAI
records.system: ChatGPT; model version not established in the recovered reporting
records.what_happened: ABC reported that ChatGPT falsely portrayed Hepburn Shire mayor Brian Hood as implicated in a foreign-bribery scandal. The report describes his actual role at Note Printing Australia as a whistleblower and prosecution witness; Hood said he had never been charged.
records.impact: Hood reported shock, sent a concerns letter and was considering defamation proceedings. The readable account does not establish a filed lawsuit, judgment or damages.
records.response: Hood told ABC that he had not yet received a response. No direct OpenAI statement was recovered; this is his account at the time of reporting.
records.response_status: Subject’s reported lack of response; no direct company statement recovered
records.prevention_analysis: Require reliable biographical evidence before producing a criminal allegation about a person. If identity, role or legal outcome cannot be verified, withhold the assertion and route it to review.
records.source_scope: Substantive indexed ABC passages, truncated; original BBC URL unreadable. Later legal outcomes and the archive’s specific prison-sentence wording were not verified.

records.title: Controlled study: ChatGPT generated fabricated bibliographic citations
records.date_basis: Experimental outputs generated in the first week of April 2023; paper published September 7, 2023.
records.organization: Walters and Wilder (researchers); ChatGPT (system evaluated)
records.system: ChatGPT-3.5 and ChatGPT-4, as named in the paper; historical test conditions
records.what_happened: Walters and Wilder tested literature-review generation on 42 topics, producing 84 texts with 636 citations. In this study’s dataset, 55% of GPT-3.5 citations and 18% of GPT-4 citations were fabricated.
records.impact: These are measured defective outputs in a controlled study. The recovered paper passages do not establish downstream publication harm, financial losses or a current model failure rate.
records.response: The recovered paper urges ongoing assessment of trust in these tools. No case-specific vendor response or corrective action was established.
records.response_status: No vendor response verified
records.prevention_analysis: Resolve each bibliography item against authoritative bibliographic records, then read the source to check claim support. Keep unresolved citations out of the finished review; ask a reviewer to resolve them.
records.source_scope: Indexed methods-period and results passages from the primary paper; complete article unavailable. Study proportions apply only to this sample and these historical systems.

records.title: ChatGPT: a fabricated article attached a false allegation to Jonathan Turley
records.date_basis: Public-report month; ABA Journal published April 6, 2023. Exact generation day unknown.
records.organization: OpenAI
records.system: ChatGPT; model version not established in the recovered reporting
records.what_happened: ABA Journal reported that ChatGPT falsely accused law professor Jonathan Turley of student sexual harassment and cited a nonexistent Washington Post article. The output also assigned the wrong university and a student trip the report says had not occurred.
records.impact: Turley described the allegation as harmful and disturbing. The readable account discusses possible libel liability, but does not establish a filed suit or awarded damages.
records.response: OpenAI said it warned users that answers could be inaccurate and was working to improve factual accuracy.
records.response_status: Response reported in the linked source
records.prevention_analysis: Require a retrievable article and a passage supporting the exact allegation, identity and institution. Block unsupported accusations instead of inventing examples to satisfy a request.
records.source_scope: Substantive indexed ABA Journal reporting with attributed company response; incomplete page. Turley’s original USA Today account was unreadable.

records.title: Park v. Kim: an unverified ChatGPT citation reaches an appeal
records.date_basis: Date of the opinion documenting the citation and referral; reply-brief filing and generation dates were not recovered.
records.organization: Counsel in Park v. Kim
records.system: ChatGPT, as identified in the opinion; model version unverified
records.what_happened: The opinion records counsel admitting that a reply brief cited a nonexistent state-court decision suggested by ChatGPT without reading or otherwise verifying it.
records.impact: The Second Circuit referred counsel to its Grievance Panel and ordered that the client receive the opinion. The underlying dismissal was affirmed for persistent violations of court orders, separately from the fabricated citation. Later disciplinary outcomes are not established here.
records.response: The opinion records counsel explaining the use of ChatGPT to find supporting precedent and arguing that courts should caution lawyers about the technology. This is a recorded explanation, not a separately verified firm or developer statement.
records.response_status: Counsel explanation recorded in the opinion; no separate developer response verified
records.prevention_analysis: Require a retrieved original decision and a checked proposition before a citation enters a filing. A generated citation without an inspectable authority must fail review. Referral and case dismissal should also be tracked separately when auditing consequences.
records.source_scope: Court opinion on Justia. Same-document indexed heading and passages about the citation, counsel explanation and consequences; full PDF and screenshot inaccessible. Batch 1 re-read corroborated the decision date and referral; the exact reply-brief date remains unrecovered.

records.title: MyCity: a government chatbot gave incorrect housing guidance
records.date_basis: Testing reported March 29, 2024, five months after the October 2023 launch; exact test days not recovered.
records.organization: New York City (operator); Microsoft (technology provider)
records.system: MyCity business chatbot; described by The Markup as Microsoft-powered
records.what_happened: The Markup tested New York City’s business chatbot and found it saying landlords need not accept Section 8 vouchers or tenants receiving rental assistance. The investigation contrasted those answers with the city’s source-of-income protections, while noting a small owner- or family-occupied-building exception.
records.impact: The readable investigation establishes misleading guidance. It does not establish that a landlord acted on the answers or that a tenant suffered a documented loss.
records.response: On April 2, Mayor Eric Adams acknowledged problems and said the service would remain available while errors were addressed. The site strengthened beta warnings and cautioned against using answers as legal or professional advice. A Microsoft response was not recovered. This describes the response then, not current service availability.
records.response_status: Response reported in the linked source
records.prevention_analysis: Produce eligibility guidance from maintained jurisdiction-specific rules, including exceptions. Require source passages supporting the exact answer and escalate unresolved legal questions instead of generating a rule.
records.source_scope: Indexed opening and housing comparison from the primary investigation; indexed April 2 response at https://themarkup.org/artificial-intelligence/2024/04/02/malfunctioning-nyc-ai-chatbot-still-active-despite-widespread-evidence-its-encouraging-illegal-behavior. Full article bodies unavailable. Other examples in the supplied brief are not imported.

records.title: Google AI Overviews: forum sarcasm becomes glue-on-pizza advice
records.date_basis: Month of the erroneous overview episode addressed by Google on May 30, 2024; exact generation date not established.
records.organization: Google
records.system: Google Search AI Overviews; exact model version not established by the passages reviewed
records.what_happened: Google acknowledged an AI Overview advising glue to make cheese stick to pizza and said some overviews incorporated sarcastic or trolling forum content. This record concerns unsupported advice presented as an answer; Google distinguishes such source misinterpretation from outright fabrication.
records.impact: Google acknowledged erroneous overviews and announced changes to when they appear and how certain sources are handled. The passages reviewed do not establish that anyone followed the advice or suffered physical harm.
records.response: Google attributed errors to misinterpreted queries, web-language nuances and gaps in reliable information. It announced better detection of nonsensical queries, limits on satire and humor, and restrictions on potentially misleading user-generated content. These are company-reported changes, not independently measured effectiveness. The May 30 response also reports additional health-related triggering safeguards; their effectiveness was not independently assessed here.
records.response_status: Direct company response; indexed substantive passages
records.prevention_analysis: A source-support check must assess whether content is serious and applicable, not just whether an answer matches a retrieved page. Withhold actionable food advice when support is sarcastic, unreliable or unresolved. Test this gate with adversarial forum and satire examples.
records.source_scope: Google response dated May 30, 2024. Indexed opening and targeted same-page passages recovered; complete body unavailable. Glue type, quantity and physical injury are not asserted. Batch 1 re-read recovered additional company response passages; previously reviewed glue-specific evidence is retained.

records.title: Sandoval appeal: ChatGPT invents witnesses and testimony
records.date_basis: The September 11, 2026 report places the described ChatGPT use in the previous year, 2025. The exact interaction and brief-filing dates were not recovered. September 2026 sanctions are a later milestone.
records.organization: Defense counsel in State v. Sandoval, New Mexico
records.system: ChatGPT; model version not verified
records.what_happened: Reuters reports that Stephen Aarons used ChatGPT to summarize trial proceedings while accepting a murder-conviction appeal. His brief included nonexistent witnesses and invented police testimony, including a fabricated description of the shooter’s clothing.
records.impact: Reuters reports a September 2026 contempt finding, a $5,000 fine and a disciplinary referral. The appeal remained pending and had been reassigned to a public defender. These are consequences for the defective briefing, not a reversal of the conviction.
records.response: Aarons expressed remorse, said he had underestimated the extent to which ChatGPT could invent facts, and characterized the episode as an honest mistake. No separate OpenAI response was verified.
records.response_status: Counsel response reported by Reuters
records.prevention_analysis: Require every asserted witness, quotation and factual description to point to a checked passage in the certified trial record. Block unsupported additions from the final signed brief.
records.source_scope: Partial Reuters reporting recovered from the exact URL; primary order unreadable. The recovered article does not establish an exact brief-filing date.

records.title: Wadsworth: lawyers sanctioned over eight nonexistent cases
records.date_basis: Sanctions-order date; offending motion’s filing date was not stated in the readable reporting.
records.organization: Morgan & Morgan (counsel associated with filing); Walmart (defendant)
records.system: AI citation-generation tool; product identity not established in the readable article
records.what_happened: Bloomberg Law reported that a motion in limine in Wadsworth v. Walmart contained eight AI-generated citations to nonexistent cases. The report identifies Rudwin Ayala as the drafter and T. Michael Morgan and Taly Goody as additional signatories.
records.impact: The court fined Ayala $3,000 and revoked his pro hac vice status in the case; Morgan and Goody were fined $1,000 each. The firm itself was not sanctioned. These amounts are from Bloomberg Law’s account of the order.
records.response: The firm acknowledged the hallucinations, apologized, withdrew the motion, introduced AI training protocols and paid opposing counsel’s fees for defending the motion. The fee amount was not stated.
records.response_status: Response reported in the linked source
records.prevention_analysis: Require every signatory to verify each cited decision and the proposition it supports before filing. Track unresolved citations and block submission until the responsible lawyer completes review.
records.source_scope: Substantive Bloomberg Law article through its concluding case reference. FindLaw’s court-opinion opening corroborates date/court but not the full incident narrative: https://caselaw.findlaw.com/court/us-dis-crt-d-wyo/117003959.html. Original PDF inaccessible; exact motion date and MX2.law identification not adopted.

records.title: Anthropic litigation: Claude returned incorrect authors and title for a citation
records.date_basis: Declaration filing date reported by Music Business Worldwide; counsel’s apology was May 15 and the article May 16, 2025.
records.organization: Anthropic; Latham & Watkins (counsel)
records.system: Claude, used to generate a research footnote according to counsel’s explanation
records.what_happened: Music Business Worldwide reported that an April 30 declaration by Anthropic employee and expert witness Olivia Chen contained a faulty research citation. Counsel said Claude generated its footnote with an incorrect title and authors for a paper Chen had located.
records.impact: The court directed preservation of information concerning the declaration, according to the report. The recovered passages do not establish a fine or sanction against Anthropic.
records.response: Counsel Ivana Dukanovic apologized on May 15, said a manual citation check had missed the error and reported added review procedures. She described it as an honest citation mistake rather than fabricated authority; that is counsel’s explanation, not an independent court finding.
records.response_status: Response reported in the linked source
records.prevention_analysis: Compare generated author, title and publication metadata directly with the source before signing a declaration. A correct link alone does not validate the rest of a citation.
records.source_scope: Substantive indexed Music Business Worldwide account, truncated. Reuters and the publishers’ CourtListener filing were unreadable. The archive’s broader three-source allegation and judicial quotations are not imported.

records.title: Johnson v. Dunn: fabricated citations in two motions
records.date_basis: Court history identifies a deposition motion filed May 7, 2025; month precision retained for the two-motion episode. Sanctions order filed July 23, 2025.
records.organization: Butler Snow LLP (counsel in Johnson v. Dunn)
records.system: ChatGPT, identified in counsel’s acknowledgements recorded by the court
records.what_happened: Recovered passages from the court’s order identify five problematic citations across two motions. Matthew B. Reeves, William J. Cranford and William R. Lunsford acknowledged in writing and at a hearing that the fabricated citations were ChatGPT hallucinations.
records.impact: The court publicly reprimanded the three lawyers, disqualified them from this case, ordered publication and referred the matter to licensing authorities. Butler Snow and two other attorneys were released without sanctions; the record does not establish a later disciplinary outcome.
records.response: The lawyers acknowledged the problem, and the firm commissioned an independent investigation. The order describes that investigation as informing the decision not to suspend them from practice throughout the district.
records.response_status: Response reported in the linked source
records.prevention_analysis: Require retrieval and reading of every authority before filing, with a recorded review by the responsible attorney. Generated confidence and a colleague’s draft are insufficient evidence that an opinion exists.
records.source_scope: Indexed primary-order passages on the procedural history, acknowledgements, sanctions and firm investigation. Complete PDF and page images unavailable.

records.title: Winters lawsuit: alleged false reassurance about worsening symptoms
records.date_basis: Month of the alleged emergency and immediately preceding interaction, supported by CBS/WCBI reporting. Reports differ from the archive on the July 2026 filing day, so that day is not used as the event date.
records.organization: OpenAI, defendant in Scott Winters’s lawsuit
records.system: ChatGPT-4o, as identified in the reported complaint
records.what_happened: CBS reporting carried by WCBI describes Winters’s allegation that ChatGPT minimized dizziness and blood-pressure instability, advised staying home in a recliner, and said more episodes were needed before his condition became serious. The report says he consulted it again hours before a July 2025 pulmonary embolism. These are allegations about unsupported medical reassurance, not adjudicated findings.
records.impact: Winters alleges he followed the advice and suffered a pulmonary embolism, and that a doctor linked immobility to the event. The sources verify reporting of the lawsuit, not medical causation or OpenAI’s liability. No judgment was verified.
records.response: CBS reports OpenAI’s position that ChatGPT is not a doctor and should not replace medical care. The retrieved material does not establish a resolution of the lawsuit.
records.response_status: Party response recorded in the cited source; access limits stated
records.prevention_analysis: Block personalized diagnostic reassurance or instructions to delay care when no qualified clinical assessment supports them. Route concerning symptom questions to appropriate clinical assessment; evaluate that escalation boundary separately from the fluency of the answer.
records.source_scope: Reported lawsuit allegation, explicitly not a finding of medical causation. Substantive WCBI-carried CBS passages support the specific statements; the complaint and full logs were unreadable. Response corroborated by https://www.cbsnews.com/news/chatgpt-dangerous-medical-advice-openai-lawsuit/.

records.title: Credit One: AI-generated submissions misdescribe legal authorities
records.date_basis: The Witness identifies this as a 2026 case in its July 18, 2026 article. Exact filing and judgment dates were not recovered; the archive's September date and neutral citation are not verified.
records.organization: Hong Kong District Court proceedings in Credit One Finance Ltd v Cheung Yiu Cho and another
records.system: Generative AI; product and version not identified in the readable source
records.what_happened: The Witness reports that the second defendant's descriptions of legal authorities did not match the judgments. It reports that the judge found false information in the submissions and that the defendant acknowledged at closing that most of the submissions were AI-generated.
records.impact: The judge rejected the submissions and emphasized litigants' personal responsibility for their legal arguments. The readable account does not establish a monetary sanction, costs amount or final appeal outcome.
records.response: The second defendant admitted that most of the submissions were AI-generated. No AI vendor was identified in the case-specific reporting and no separate vendor response was recovered.
records.response_status: Participant response reported by the linked news source; no separate vendor statement recovered
records.prevention_analysis: Require the original judgment for every legal citation and compare the cited passage with the proposition before filing. Block unresolved citations and retain the review evidence. This is a proposed verification control, not proof of prevention in the original proceeding.
records.source_scope: Substantive indexed article text recovered after the initial opening failed; not the underlying judgment. Publication timestamp: July 18, 2026, 01:46. Article names the case and year but not an exact decision date or individual fabricated case names. The archive's HKDC citation and additional details remain unverified.

records.title: Mazaheri: unchecked AI authorities aggravate a tribunal costs award
records.date_basis: Decision year from the neutral citation 2026 ONLSTH 112. Law Times reported it on June 17, 2026, but the ruling and filing dates were not recovered; the reporting date is not used as the event date.
records.organization: Self-represented counsel in Mazaheri v. Law Society of Ontario
records.system: Grok, identified in Gardiner Roberts’ account; model version not established
records.what_happened: Law Times reports that Shahryar Mazaheri used unchecked AI output in four filings, citing nonexistent cases and real cases that did not support the propositions advanced. Gardiner Roberts identifies Grok as the tool used for the motion materials.
records.impact: Law Times reports $31,150 in costs payable to the Law Society of Ontario, with irresponsible AI use treated as an aggravating factor. The recovered evidence does not establish that the entire award was caused by AI errors. The earlier licence suspension is not attributed to AI in this record.
records.response: The readable Law Times and Gardiner Roberts passages did not contain Mazaheri’s response to the problematic authorities. No apology, explanation or developer response is asserted here.
records.response_status: Response not recovered in the sources reviewed
records.prevention_analysis: Before submitting a tribunal motion, retrieve every cited decision and check both its identity and the proposition attributed to it. A hyperlink resolving to a different real case must fail review just as a nonexistent case does.
records.source_scope: Partial indexed Law Times reporting and Gardiner Roberts analysis: https://www.mondaq.com/canada/information-technology/1808888/the-costs-of-cutting-corners-with-ai-mazaheri-v-law-society-of-ontario. CanLII decision 2026 ONLSTH 112 could not be read. Tool attribution is secondary reporting; cost allocation and personal response were not recovered.

records.title: Full Fact trial: chatbots repeat false claims and misidentify images
records.date_basis: The primary report says testing began in February 2026 and covers its first five months. Month precision is retained; August 28 publication and September 2 update are later milestones.
records.organization: Full Fact, testing Google, OpenAI and xAI systems
records.system: Gemini, ChatGPT and Grok via API; complete model/version list not recovered
records.what_happened: Full Fact reported false factual responses during a five-month fact-checking trial, including a fabricated account of a confrontation in Parliament and misidentification of fire footage and an AI-generated Earth image. It reported 39 major errors across 67 incorrect responses. These are distinct counts, not an error-rate denominator.
records.impact: Some responses corrected after Full Fact published fact checks; others remained wrong. The trial establishes false test responses, not quantified downstream harm, a representative hallucination rate or proof that chatbots originated the underlying misinformation.
records.response: OpenAI said it took the examples seriously and distinguished API testing from ordinary consumer ChatGPT use. Google objected to the developer-channel setup and use of older models, and said later website checks debunked the claims. An xAI response was not recovered.
records.response_status: Company responses recorded in Full Fact’s primary trial report
records.prevention_analysis: Require evidence for each factual assertion, especially image provenance and breaking-news claims. Abstain when provenance is unresolved, and retest after corrections using a versioned evaluation set and recorded model settings.
records.source_scope: Partial primary trial report and targeted exact-page response passages. The complete model list, exact trial end date and full test corpus were not recovered.

records.title: Barteca v. Tacobarn: real cases receive unsupported quotations
records.date_basis: April 21, 2026 is the dismissal-motion filing date explicitly recovered from the order. The sanctions decision followed on August 4.
records.organization: Defense counsel for Tacobarn entities in Barteca Holdings litigation
records.system: Generative AI; individual tool attribution omitted from this scoped record
records.what_happened: The court’s recovered passages identify quotations absent from the cited Iqbal page, a misrepresentation of Streetwise as addressing incontestability, and incorrect page references in a dismissal motion. The order attributes unverified generative-AI use to defense counsel Hilary Miller.
records.impact: ABA Journal reports a $3,500 sanction, referral to the Federal Grievance Committee and removal of the defective filings. The August 4 sanctions decision does not establish the ultimate outcome of the trademark claims.
records.response: ABA Journal reports Miller’s remorse and promised changes to his verification process. His complete account of the tools and checking steps was not recovered.
records.response_status: Counsel response reported by ABA Journal
records.prevention_analysis: Verify the exact quotation and the proposition it supports in the original opinion. A case’s existence or a valid page reference alone should not pass the filing review.
records.source_scope: Partial primary order passages confirm April 21 filing and specific errors. EDRM corroborates the August 4 decision date; ABA Journal supplies sanctions and response. All three sources are listed on the Tracker.

records.title: Lnu: fabricated appellate authorities and inaccurate explanations draw suspensions
records.date_basis: Opinion filing date shown in the court caption and corroborated by ABA Journal; original brief filing dates were not recovered.
records.organization: Counsel in Lnu v. Blanche before the Ninth Circuit
records.system: Generative AI; the court summary attributes the errors to AI, while counsel described unauthorized use by brief writers as probable; product unknown
records.what_happened: The court-staff summary describes briefs with nonexistent cases, misattributed quotations and misrepresentations of real authorities. ABA Journal reports that attorneys Mike Singh Sethi and William Rounds initially blamed typographical errors and eventually acknowledged probable unauthorized AI use by brief writers.
records.impact: ABA Journal reports a $2,500 sanction against each attorney, six-month suspensions from Ninth Circuit practice and a two-year AI-use disclosure requirement. These measures concern the filings and subsequent explanations; they do not establish a general prohibition on AI research.
records.response: According to ABA Journal, the attorneys admitted failing to check citations after initially denying AI involvement. The court said earlier disclosure and an apology might have warranted lesser sanctions. No separate firm or developer statement was verified.
records.response_status: Counsel’s explanations reported by ABA Journal; court-staff summary corroborates the misconduct and suspension
records.prevention_analysis: Give the signing lawyer a complete evidence checklist for every authority, regardless of who drafted the brief. Require original-source review and preserve unresolved discrepancies; correction workflows should accurately disclose what is known about provenance.
records.source_scope: Primary caption and staff summary recovered, not the full opinion. Sanction amounts, disclosure period and counsel’s probable-use wording come from substantive ABA Journal reporting: https://www.abajournal.com/news/article/attorneys-lack-of-candor-over-ai-errors-leads-to-stricter-sanctions.

records.title: Withers: unverified AI authorities reach filings from both sides
records.date_basis: Date of the sanctions order reported by Mississippi Free Press; the original filing dates were not established in the readable source.
records.organization: Counsel for Tom Withers III and the City of Aberdeen
records.system: Generative AI in legal memoranda, according to Mississippi Free Press; products not established by the recovered passages
records.what_happened: Mississippi Free Press reports fabricated authorities in a fee-dispute case involving Tom Withers III and the City of Aberdeen. Its quoted court passage says all four attorneys failed to verify authorities, violating Rule 11.
records.impact: The article reports that Judge Sharion Aycock’s June 8 order removed all four lawyers and barred two from practice in the Northern District of Mississippi for two years. Monetary amounts and the identities of the two subject to the district-wide bars were not recovered and are not specified here.
records.response: According to the article, local counsel Ridgeway and McClinton denied personally using AI but had not adequately reviewed the memoranda prepared by Wilson and Williams. Further explanations or a tool-provider response were not recovered.
records.response_status: Local counsel explanations reported in news coverage; other responses unavailable in recovered text
records.prevention_analysis: Require every signing or sponsoring lawyer to verify the authorities they adopt, with evidence shared across local and lead counsel. A delegated drafting task should not bypass the filing gate or turn another person’s unchecked output into approved authority.
records.source_scope: Substantive indexed news reporting and a quoted court finding; full article and court order not recovered. Product names, original brief dates, individual fine amounts and additional explanations in the archive are excluded.

records.title: Landberg: fabricated authorities in an appellate brief lead to sanctions
records.date_basis: Date of the sanctions decision as reported by Marshall Dennehey; brief filing and model-generation dates were not recovered.
records.organization: Plaintiff’s counsel and law firm in Landberg v. City of New York
records.system: Generative AI, as counsel later acknowledged in the reported proceedings; product not established
records.what_happened: Marshall Dennehey’s account of the Second Department decision reports three nonexistent cases and misrepresented holdings in the plaintiff’s brief. Counsel initially attributed the citations to conventional research and later acknowledged AI hallucination.
records.impact: The article reports an $8,000 sanction against counsel and $2,500 against the firm. Defense counsel were criticized for not flagging the fabrications but were not sanctioned in this account.
records.response: The reported proceedings record counsel declining a recess to investigate the citations and later acknowledging their AI origin. The article says the firm had policies against this use. A separate firm or AI-provider statement was not recovered.
records.response_status: Counsel explanation and firm policy reported in legal analysis; no separate provider response verified
records.prevention_analysis: Require each appellate authority and quoted proposition to be checked against the original opinion before filing. An unresolved citation should block submission and trigger a documented correction, even when another reviewer has already signed off.
records.source_scope: Substantive indexed legal analysis of the decision, not a complete court-order read. The NYSBA digest was also partially recovered: https://nysba.org/web-post-new-york-state-law-digest-august-2026/. The record does not rely on snippet-only details or identify a model.

records.title: Akerlund: a response to false citations contains another set of false cases
records.date_basis: July 2026 decision milestone in reporting published July 10, which calls it Friday’s decision. Exact filing dates were not recovered; the entry retains month precision.
records.organization: Counsel for aviation employees in Akerlund v. Atlas Air, Inc.
records.system: AI software identified in the reported judicial findings; vendor and model not named
records.what_happened: Bloomberg Law reports that Anthony F. Sabatini’s opening brief contained at least eight fabricated case citations. records.title: ChatGPT cartoon falsely carries Brendan Loper’s signature
records.date_basis: August 26 is the posting date shown in the investigation’s image caption. The report was published October 5; the exact image-generation date is unknown.
records.organization: OpenAI, ChatGPT
records.system: ChatGPT image generation; model version not verified
records.what_happened: Nieman Lab reported that a ChatGPT-generated cartoon carried Brendan Loper’s signature although he neither drew nor signed it. The person who generated it reportedly asked for a New Yorker-style cartoon. This record concerns false authorship attribution, not evidence that the named artist approved the image.
records.impact: Nieman Lab reported circulation of the image and inquiries to Loper from relatives and strangers. No financial-loss amount is established. This entry does not reproduce the cartoon or assert that all similar requests produce signatures.
records.response: OpenAI said its tools aim to support human creativity and welcomed reports of bugs and unintended behavior. Mashable’s follow-up distinguishes that statement from a chatbot guardrail warning and reports continued signature generation; the reporting does not establish a complete fix.
records.response_status: Company spokesperson response reported by Mashable
records.prevention_analysis: Do not treat a generated name or signature as proof of authorship. Block publication of an image carrying a real person’s attribution unless provenance and authorization are verified.
records.source_scope: Partial Nieman Lab investigation supports the specific example and image-caption date. OpenAI response recovered in Mashable’s Yahoo-hosted report, linked in the response field.

records.title: CivilNet study: chatbots repeat unsupported claims about artists' political statements
records.date_basis: Publication milestone of the Armenian article: header reads September 14, 12:28; 2026 is inferred from its March 2026 chronology and testing months later. Exact test dates are unknown. This differs from the archive's September 25 label.
records.organization: CivilNetCheck (research); OpenAI, Google, xAI and Anthropic (tested chatbot providers)
records.system: ChatGPT, Gemini, Grok and Claude; precise model versions and configurations not verified
records.what_happened: CivilNetCheck reports asking four chatbots in Armenian, Russian and English whether internationally recognized artists had criticized Armenia's prime minister. Eleven of 24 answers said yes. The authors labelled example answers from Gemini, Claude and ChatGPT false, including Claude's attribution of criticism to Serj Tankian. They reported finding no such Tankian statement; that search finding is not conclusive proof that no statement existed.
records.impact: The documented result is a set of answers the researchers classified as false or unsupported. The recovered passages do not establish downstream harm, a population-wide error rate, or how the claims entered the systems. The complete checking methodology was not recovered.
records.response: The article says CivilNet sent inquiries to OpenAI, Google, xAI and Anthropic on publication day and would publish answers when received. No substantive vendor answer or later correction was recovered in this review.
records.response_status: Study authors report inquiries sent; no vendor response recovered
records.prevention_analysis: Before attributing political statements to a named person, retrieve the original statement and verify speaker, wording and context. If that evidence is missing, withhold the attribution rather than extrapolating from a narrative. Evaluate this gate across languages; this is an editorial proposal, not a tested result of the study.
records.source_scope: Partial indexed passages from the Armenian article, including the experiment examples, header and vendor-inquiry note. English URL was unreadable. Year is supported by article chronology rather than printed in the recovered header. The archive's wider 504-prompt metrics and exact model versions were not independently recovered and are omitted.

records.title: KVA study: chatbots describe unlicensed casinos as licensed
records.date_basis: Study-publication milestone: KVA’s October 15, 2026 release says the study was published September 30. Exact testing dates were not recovered; this is not a dated consumer transaction.
records.organization: Keurmerk Verantwoorde Affiliates (KVA); Google, Microsoft and Mistral tools in its study
records.system: Google Gemini, Microsoft Copilot and Mistral Le Chat; versions not verified
records.what_happened: KVA reported that Gemini, Copilot and Le Chat presented gambling providers without Dutch licences as legal or licensed by the Dutch regulator. All ten tested tools named unlicensed providers, but naming one was not always an endorsement: some responses discussed enforcement. The licensing misrepresentations, rather than every operator mention, are the scoped failure.
records.impact: The release describes a bounded sample of 79 recorded AI responses. It demonstrates reported output errors, not measured gambling losses, affected minors or a comparative safety ranking. The study was not independently repeated for this Tracker.
records.response: KVA urged developers to verify licensing claims against official sources. No response or remediation from the named AI providers was recovered.
records.response_status: Research publisher’s recommendation recovered; provider responses unavailable
records.prevention_analysis: Resolve licensing status against the regulator’s current register before making a legal-status claim. Preserve the jurisdiction and verification date, and withhold assurance when a matching licensed operator cannot be established.
records.source_scope: Substantive indexed KVA press release dated October 15, 2026; underlying study PDF unavailable. NL Times separately reports the licensing misrepresentations: https://nltimes.nl/2026/10/03/10-ai-chatbots-tested-point-consumers-unlicensed-online-gambling-sites . Testing dates and provider responses were not recovered.
